title: MSHA enforcement citations
summary: Research task: predict whether a US mine safety inspection will cite a given 30 CFR section - one binary task instance per section, over 26 years of federal enforcement records.

post.title: A citation-prediction task from MSHA's enforcement record
paragraphs: This release packages 497,897 mine inspections into 45 per-section research tasks. Inspection start is the intended prediction instant. History is ordered by earlier inspection start dates, which does not establish that those inspections' citations were already available; current mine attributes also lack historical-vintage verification. The original leakage checks missed later-row outcome exposure, now documented in the suitability notice.

The task is binary and per-section: will this inspection cite 30 CFR 56.12004? The label is the set of sections the inspector actually wrote, taken from the violation rows, so this is an enforcement outcome - what the inspector found - and not a hazard measurement. Each of the 45 shipped sections is a complete task instance over the identical pool: train 2001-2020, eval 2021-2023, holdout 2024-2025.

The numbers are published with their floor. On the reference section sec_56_12004 the baseline reaches 0.8036 eval AUC, identical from the training path and an independent validation re-run. The persistence reference - the same model using only whether that section was cited at the mine's previous inspection - reaches 0.5831, so the full feature set clears it by 0.2205. Section prevalence ranges around 9-11% on the reference task; score AUC, not accuracy.

limitations: A derived research dataset from MSHA public-domain data, labelled as derived - not an official MSHA or Department of Labor product.
The label is an enforcement outcome: what an inspector cited, not a measured hazard. Mines that are inspected more often generate more citations.
Only sections cited in at least 1% of pooled inspections ship as configs, so this is not a census of 30 CFR.

A mine is the same entity across splits by design - prior history is the point of the task. The temporal split is what prevents leakage, and the holdout is labelled and downloadable: keep its labels outside an evaluated agent's workspace.

No claim of real-time or operational forecasting validity: historical feature and label availability at the prediction instant is assumed from a current source snapshot, not verified against release vintages.

The labeled eval split is development/validation. Final holdout scoring requires prediction-time access restrictions; the original scorer provided the complete feature frame. Downloadable holdout labels must stay outside model development.
baseline_scope: One baseline through the runner's training and validation contract. No agent or harness comparison was run and none is implied.
